text.p: A wave of kidnappings in Tajikistan shows the former Soviet republic is prey to a confusing array of armed bands, dimming hopes for peace.
Diplomats based in the mountainous republic of 5.7 million fear that simmering clan rivalries could restart the four-year civil war which government and Islamic guerrillas agreed to end in December.

The Islamic opposition has for years operated out of bases in neighbouring Afghanistan and its fighters, sporting brown pancake hats, long beards and religious amulets, closely resemble the Afghan mujahideen across the border.

The armed faction that grabbed foreign aid workers and journalists earlier this week once fought for the opposition and its main demand is safe passage back to Tajikistan for members of the group still based in northern Afghanistan.
"You have guys here who have had experience in Afghanistan which to some extent has impacted on this conflict," said a Western diplomat in Dushanbe.
He said the main danger threatening Tajikistan's peace accord was clan struggle over the impoverished country's spoils -- some gold, a fast-declining cotton crop, aluminium and narcotics.
Tajikistan's web of clan and political rivalries is mind-bending at the best of times.

In this week's hostage-taking, the kidnappers, loyal to warlord Rizvon Sadirov, said they had switched allegiance from the Islamic guerrillas to secular Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov at the end of last year.

With friends like Sadirov, say observers, Rakhmonov does not need enemies. But the Tajik leader, who has pledged to negotiate the release of the hostages, is constantly putting out political fires in his own back yard while trying to be tough in negotiations with his Islamic foes at the same time.

Only last month, the commander of his elite armoured brigade moved his tanks on an aluminium-producing town held by a rival warlord without notifying Rakhmonov, the nominal head of Tajikistan's scrappy armed forces.
The ambitious Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, now high on diplomats' lists of potential coup-makers, refused repeated orders to return to barracks and rumbled back to base at his leisure.
Western observers estimate Rakhmonov only controls about 15-20 percent of the republic, with around half in the hands of the Islamic guerrillas.

"These incidents are frustrating as we are getting good vibes from both sides (government and opposition) on the peace talks," said the western diplomat. Another round of talks is scheduled to take place in Moscow on February 26.
The roller-coaster politics in the far-flung republic attracts little attention in western chancelleries.
But its Central Asian neighbours and former colonial overlord Russia nurse an acute fear that Afghan-style instability could spread northwards through the region via Tajikistan.
The Kremlin has tried to throw up a wall against radical Islam by stationing around 20,000 troops in the country to carry out peace-keeping duties and guard the border with Afghanistan.

But Russian soldiers are themselves victims of ambushes, shootings and booby-trapped cars and their presence is resented by the Tajik opposition, who are now negotiating a power-sharing arrangement with Rakhmonov.
"Rakhmonov is only in place thanks to Russian bayonets," grumbled one opposition official.
